title: The Real Leadership Differentiator
author: Business Leader Daily
summary: This Business Leader Daily issue argues that what separates great leaders from good ones is not innate talent, an advantaged background, or the right early mentors, but a daily, unglamorous commitment to refining the craft of leadership. Great leaders read, ask questions, invite feedback, and track what worked and why — not out of ego but out of a wish to be better tomorrow than today. The piece cites McKinsey's CEO Excellence research (nearly 8,000 chief executives) finding that leaders who sustained performance past their early tenure consistently enhanced their own learning agendas, while those who grew comfortable lost ground. Its central image is compounding: one good book a quarter or one acted-upon piece of feedback feels inconsequential in the moment but, stacked over five and ten years, separates leaders from their former peers. The uncomfortable corollary is that leadership never arrives — the day you decide you've learned enough is the day you start sliding backward.
points: The real differentiator is not talent, background or mentors but a daily commitment to refining the craft of leadership.
McKinsey's CEO Excellence research on nearly 8,000 executives found those who sustained performance kept enhancing their learning agendas, while the comfortable ones lost ground.
The compounding of small inputs — a book a quarter, a monthly mentor conversation, acted-upon feedback — is 'the whole game,' separating leaders from former peers over years.
Leadership never arrives: the day you decide you've learned enough is the day you start sliding backward, and people feel it before you do.
quotes: Strip away the polish, and you find something less glamorous: a daily commitment to refining the craft.

After studying nearly 8,000 chief executives, the authors found that the leaders who sustained performance past their early tenure did one thing consistently. They enhanced their own learning agendas.
Ten years later, they’ve separated you from the people who were once your peers. The math is unforgiving in both directions.
The day you decide you’ve learned enough is the day you start sliding backward, and the people around you feel it long before you do.
If you want to know who’s still worth following five years from now, watch what they do when no one is asking them to grow.
What actually differentiates the expert performers from the good performers is their dedication to doing something every day to improve.
